claims.text: Adding 0.5–1 at% boron to phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys will improve their glass-forming ability.
Adding 0.5–1 at% boron will enhance the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
Minor boron addition will produce locally stable B–P clusters.
Locally stable B–P clusters hinder crystallization.
Undoped phosphorus-containing alloys such as Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-P have a relatively narrow supercooled-liquid region.
Undoped phosphorus-containing alloys such as Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-P have lower crystallization-onset temperatures than the proposed boron-doped alloys.
Induction melting followed by conventional inert-atmosphere melt quenching can homogeneously incorporate 0.5–1 at% boron into the alloy.
B–P clusters act as pinning centers that reduce atomic mobility.
Boron has a strong chemical affinity for phosphorus in the proposed alloy context.
Reduced atomic mobility caused by B–P clusters disrupts nucleation during cooling.
Reduced atomic mobility caused by B–P clusters disrupts crystal growth during cooling.
B–P clustering decreases the effective critical cooling rate required for vitrification.
B–P clustering delays crystallization onset during subsequent heating.
The boron-doped alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than an otherwise comparably processed undoped alloy.
The boron-doped alloy will have a broader supercooled-liquid region than an otherwise comparably processed undoped alloy.
The beneficial effect is limited to a boron concentration of 0.5–1 at%.
Significantly higher boron concentrations may produce secondary crystalline phases.
Non-homogeneous mixing may prevent the desired B–P clustering and associated improvement.
